entries.content_plain: 2. Now the names of the twelve apostles are these-- The other Evangelists enumerate the twelve in immediate connection with their appointment ( Mr 3:13-19 ; Lu 6:13-16 ). And as in the Acts ( Ac 1:13 ) we have a list of the Eleven who met daily in the upper room with the other disciples after their Master's ascension until the day of Pentecost, we have four catalogues in all for comparison. The first, Simon, who is called Peter-- (See on Joh 1:42 ). and Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother-- named after James, as the younger of the two.

Philip and Bartholomew--</hi>That this person is the same with "Nathanael of Cana in Galilee" is justly concluded for the three following reasons: First, because Bartholomew is not so properly an individual's name as a family surname; next, because not only in this list, but in Mark's and Luke's (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.18">Mr 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.6.14">Lu 6:14</reference>), he follows the name of "Philip," who was the instrument of bringing Nathanael first to Jesus (<reference osisRef="John.1.45">Joh 1:45</reference>); and again, when our Lord, after His resurrection, appeared at the Sea of Tiberias, "Nathanael of Cana in Galilee" is mentioned along with six others, all of them apostles, as being present (<reference osisRef="John.21.2">Joh 21:2</reference>).<div eID="gen25785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25786" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Matthew the publican--</hi>In none of the four lists of the Twelve is this apostle so branded but in his own, as if he would have all to know how deep a debtor he had been to his Lord. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.1.3">Mt 1:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.6">5, 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.9">9:9</reference>).<div eID="gen25786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25787" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">James the son of Alphaeus--</hi>the same person apparently who is called Cleopas or Clopas (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.18">Lu 24:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.19.25">Joh 19:25</reference>); and, as he was the husband of Mary, sister to the Virgin, James the Less must have been our Lord's cousin.<div eID="gen25787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25788" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus--</hi>the same, without doubt, as "Judas the brother of James," mentioned in both the lists of Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.16">Lu 6:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.1.13">Ac 1:13</reference>), while no one of the name of Lebbaeus or Thaddaeus is so. Simon the Canaanite--</hi>rather "Kananite," but better still, "the Zealot," as he is called in <reference osisRef="Luke.6.15">Lu 6:15</reference>, where the original term should not have been retained as in our version ("Simon, called Zelotes"), but rendered "Simon, called the Zealot." The word "Kananite" is just the Aramaic, or Syro-Chaldaic, term for "Zealot." Probably before his acquaintance with Jesus, he belonged to the sect of the Zealots, who bound themselves, as a sort of voluntary ecclesiastical police, to see that the law was not broken with impunity.<div eID="gen25789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25790" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and Judas Iscariot--</hi>that is, Judas of Kerioth, a town of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.25">Jos 15:25</reference>); so called to distinguish him from "Judas the brother of James" (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.16">Lu 6:16</reference>).<div eID="gen25790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25791" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who also betrayed him--</hi>a note of infamy attached to his name in all the catalogues of the Twelve.<div eID="gen25791" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.10.5-Matt.10.42">Mt 10:5-42</reference>. The Twelve Receive Their Instructions.</title> <div sID="gen25792" type="x-p"/> This directory divides itself into three distinct parts. The first part (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.5-Matt.10.15">Mt 10:5-15</reference>) contains directions for the brief and temporary mission on which they were now going forth, with respect to the places they were to go to, the works they were to do, the message they were to bear, and the manner in which they were to conduct themselves. The second part (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.16-Matt.10.23">Mt 10:16-23</reference>) contains directions of no such limited and temporary nature, but opens out into the permanent exercise of the Gospel ministry. The third part (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.24-Matt.10.42">Mt 10:24-42</reference>) is of wider application still, reaching not only to the ministry of the Gospel in every age, but to the service of Christ in the widest sense. It is a strong confirmation of this threefold division, that each part closes with the words, "Verily I SAY UNTO YOU" (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.15">Mt 10:15</reference>, 23, 42).<div eID="gen25792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25793" type="x-p"/> Directions for the Present Mission (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.5-Matt.10.15">Mt 10:5-15</reference>). <div eID="gen25793" type="x-p"/>

These twelve Jesus sent forth, and commanded them, saying, Go not into the way of the Gentiles, and into any city of the Samaritans enter ye not--</hi>The Samaritans were Gentiles by blood; but being the descendants of those whom the king of Assyria had transported from the East to supply the place of the ten tribes carried captive, they had adopted the religion of the Jews, though with admixtures of their own: and, as the nearest neighbors of the Jews, they occupied a place intermediate between them and the Gentiles. This, though applicable to all time, and exemplified by our Lord Himself once and again, had special reference to the brief opportunities which Israel was to have of "knowing the time of His visitations." for verily I say unto you-- what will startle you, but at the same time show you the solemnity of your mission, and the need of economizing the time for it. Ye shall not have gone over-- Ye shall in nowise have completed. the cities of Israel, till the Son of man be come-- To understand this--as Lange and others do--in the first instance, of Christ's own peregrinations, as if He had said, "Waste not your time upon hostile places, for I Myself will be after you ere your work be over"--seems almost trifling. And he that taketh not his cross, and followeth after me, is not worthy of me--</hi>a saying which our Lord once and again emphatically reiterates (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.24">Mt 16:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.9.23">Lu 9:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.14.27">14:27</reference>). We have become so accustomed to this expression--"taking up one's cross"--in the sense of "being prepared for trials in general for Christ's sake," that we are apt to lose sight of its primary and proper sense here--"a preparedness to go forth even to crucifixion," as when our Lord had to bear His own cross on His way to Calvary--a saying the more remarkable as our Lord had not as yet given a hint that He would die this death, nor was crucifixion a Jewish mode of capital punishment. <div eID="gen25864" type="x-p"/>

The pith of such paradoxical maxims depends on the double sense attached to the word "life"--a lower and a higher, the natural and the spiritual, the temporal and eternal. entries.content_plain: 42. And whosoever shall give to drink unto one of these little ones-- Beautiful epithet! Originally taken from Zec 13:7 . The reference is to their lowliness in spirit, their littleness in the eyes of an undiscerning world, while high in Heaven's esteem. a cup of cold water only-- meaning, the smallest service. in the name of a disciple-- or, as it is in Mark ( Mr 9:41 ), because ye are Christ's: from love to Me, and to him from his connection with Me. verily I say unto you, he shall in no wise lose his reward-- There is here a descending climax--"a prophet," "a righteous man," "a little one"; signifying that however low we come down in our services to those that are Christ's, all that is done for His sake, and that bears the stamp of love to His blessed name, shall be divinely appreciated and owned and rewarded.
